library(dplyr)
library(tidyr)
library(readr)

library(urca)
library(changepoint)
library(knitr)

source("R/ariel-functions.R")

ar_f    <- function(x, d = 2) formatC(x, format = "f", digits = d)

# Quarterly panel: the team's 4.3 data objects from R/data.R, tsibbles indexed
# by Quarter (yearquarter), with columns date, CPI, Inflation, Unemployment
# and Treasury.
ar_quarterly <- quarterly_data
ar_initial   <- initial_data
stopifnot(nrow(ar_initial) == 160)

                   Treasury     = "3-month Treasury bill rate (%)")

## 4.1 Purpose

Stage 2 compares inflation forecasts using the corrected Stage 1 data, with every series taken as the end-of-quarter value of the monthly FRED series and inflation computed as $\pi_t=400\log(P_t/P_{t-1})$ from CPIAUCSL. We check stationarity over 1960Q1–1999Q4 (4.2), set up an expanding-window experiment (4.3), build the seven core models from Faust and Wright (2013) (4.4), and compare their forecasts through 2019Q4 (4.5). Lastly, we diagnose the best one-step model (4.6) and summarize the results (4.7).

## 4.2 Assess stationarity and structural change

We use the initial period, 1960Q1–1999Q4 (160 quarters), for every test in this section. @fig-ariel-levels shows the three series, with the segment means from a change-point analysis of inflation described below, and @fig-ariel-acf shows their autocorrelation functions.

```{r ariel-breaks}
# cpt.mean() assumes unit noise variance, so we divide by a robust estimate
# of the quarter-to-quarter noise scale before running PELT.
ar_noise_scale <- function(x) mad(diff(x)) / sqrt(2)

ar_segments_for <- function(x, dates, scale = 1) {
  cp    <- cpt.mean(x / scale, method = "PELT", penalty = "BIC")
  ends  <- c(cpts(cp), length(x))
  start <- c(1, head(ends, -1) + 1)
  tibble(start = dates[start], end = dates[ends],
         mean = param.est(cp)$mean * scale)
}

ar_pi_scale  <- ar_noise_scale(ar_initial$Inflation)
ar_segs      <- ar_segments_for(ar_initial$Inflation, ar_initial$date, ar_pi_scale)
ar_n_raw     <- nrow(ar_segments_for(ar_initial$Inflation, ar_initial$date)) - 1  # Stage 1
ar_n_scaled  <- nrow(ar_segs) - 1
ar_n_other   <- sapply(c("Unemployment", "Treasury"), function(v)
  nrow(ar_segments_for(ar_initial[[v]], ar_initial$date,
                    ar_noise_scale(ar_initial[[v]]))) - 1)

ar_seg_mean <- function(from, to) ar_segs$mean[ar_segs$start >= as.Date(from) &
                                           ar_segs$end <= as.Date(to)]
ar_high <- ar_seg_mean("1973-01-01", "1981-09-30")
ar_low  <- ar_seg_mean("1981-10-01", "1999-12-31")
# The prose names the first two segments and then these two groups, so every
# segment must fall in exactly one of them.
stopifnot(length(ar_high) + length(ar_low) + 2 == nrow(ar_segs))
ar_join_and <- function(x) if (length(x) < 2) x else
  paste0(paste(head(x, -1), collapse = ", "), " and ", tail(x, 1))
```

```{r fig-ariel-levels}
#| fig-cap: "The three series, 1960Q1–1999Q4. Dashed red lines in the inflation panel are PELT segment means after rescaling inflation by its noise scale."
#| fig-height: 4.6
ar_initial |>
  as_tibble() |>
  pivot_longer(c(Inflation, Unemployment, Treasury), names_to = "series") |>
  mutate(series = factor(series, names(ar_series_labels), ar_series_labels)) |>
  ggplot(aes(date, value)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.4) +
  geom_segment(data = ar_segs |>
                 mutate(series = factor("Inflation", names(ar_series_labels),
                                        ar_series_labels)),
               aes(x = start, xend = end, y = mean, yend = mean),
               colour = "firebrick", linetype = "dashed", linewidth = 0.6) +
  facet_wrap(~ series, ncol = 1, scales = "free_y") +
  labs(x = NULL, y = NULL,
       title = "Inflation, unemployment and the Treasury bill rate",
       subtitle = "Quarterly, 1960Q1 to 1999Q4, with PELT segment means for inflation")
```

```{r fig-ariel-acf}
#| fig-cap: "Sample ACFs of the three series in levels, lags 1–20. Dashed lines are approximate 95% bounds."
#| fig-height: 3.2
ar_acf_df <- bind_rows(lapply(names(ar_series_labels), function(v) {
  a <- acf(ar_initial[[v]], lag.max = 20, plot = FALSE)
  tibble(series = v, lag = a$lag[-1], acf = a$acf[-1])
})) |> mutate(series = factor(series, names(ar_series_labels), ar_series_labels))

ggplot(ar_acf_df, aes(lag, acf)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linewidth = 0.3) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = c(-1, 1) * 1.96 / sqrt(nrow(ar_initial)),
             linetype = "dashed", colour = "steelblue") +
  geom_segment(aes(xend = lag, yend = 0)) +
  facet_wrap(~ series, nrow = 1) +
  labs(x = "Lag (quarters)", y = "ACF",
       title = "Autocorrelation of the series in levels, 1960Q1 to 1999Q4")

ar_acf_at <- function(v, k) acf(ar_initial[[v]], lag.max = k, plot = FALSE)$acf[k + 1]
```

**What the plots show.** Inflation rises from about 1% in the early 1960s to double digits in 1974 and 1979–80, then falls back after 1981. Its ACF starts at `r ar_f(ar_acf_at("Inflation", 1))` and is still `r ar_f(ar_acf_at("Inflation", 8))` at lag 8, so dependence is persistent, but it decays steadily rather than staying near one. Unemployment and the Treasury bill rate are more persistent still, with lag-1 autocorrelations of `r ar_f(ar_acf_at("Unemployment", 1))` and `r ar_f(ar_acf_at("Treasury", 1))`. Unemployment moves in long cyclical swings, and the bill rate tracks inflation upward before spiking during the 1979–82 Volcker tightening. None of the three series returns quickly to a single fixed level.

**Unit-root tests.** For each series we run the augmented Dickey–Fuller (ADF) test with a constant and no trend, since none of these rates has an economic reason to trend deterministically. We choose the augmentation lag from 0–4 by BIC, comparing all five regressions on the same estimation sample so the BIC values are comparable, and then run `urca::ur.df()` at the selected lag. We don't use the `selectlags = "BIC"` option in `ur.df()` here, since it only searches lags 1 through the maximum and can't select 0. The KPSS test uses a constant (`type = "mu"`) and the short Newey–West bandwidth of `r ur.kpss(ar_initial$Inflation, type = "mu", lags = "short")@lag` lags, and we repeat it with the long bandwidth of `r ur.kpss(ar_initial$Inflation, type = "mu", lags = "long")@lag` lags as a robustness check. The ADF null hypothesis is a unit root, and the KPSS null hypothesis is stationarity. When the level results support a unit root, we repeat both tests on the first difference. @tbl-ariel-stationarity collects the results.

```{r ariel-unit-root}
ar_adf_lag_bic <- function(x, max_lag = 4) {
  dx  <- diff(x)
  idx <- (max_lag + 1):length(dx)          # common sample for every lag
  bic <- sapply(0:max_lag, function(k) {
    X <- cbind(level = x[idx],
               if (k > 0) sapply(1:k, function(j) dx[idx - j]))
    BIC(lm(dx[idx] ~ X))
  })
  which.min(bic) - 1
}

ar_run_tests <- function(x) {
  k        <- ar_adf_lag_bic(x)
  adf_fit  <- ur.df(x, type = "drift", lags = k)
  kpss_fit <- ur.kpss(x, type = "mu", lags = "short")
  kpss_lng <- ur.kpss(x, type = "mu", lags = "long")
  tibble(lag = k,
         adf = adf_fit@teststat[1, "tau2"],
         adf_cv = adf_fit@cval["tau2", "5pct"],
         kpss = kpss_fit@teststat, kpss_cv = kpss_fit@cval[1, "5pct"],
         kpss_cv1 = kpss_fit@cval[1, "1pct"],
         kpss_long = kpss_lng@teststat)
}

ar_ur_tbl <- bind_rows(lapply(names(ar_series_labels), function(v) {
  lev <- ar_run_tests(ar_initial[[v]]) |> mutate(series = v, form = "Level")
  if (lev$adf < lev$adf_cv) return(lev)  # unit root rejected: no differencing
  bind_rows(lev, ar_run_tests(diff(ar_initial[[v]])) |>
              mutate(series = v, form = "First difference"))
})) |>
  mutate(adf_reject = adf < adf_cv, kpss_reject = kpss > kpss_cv,
         kpss_long_reject = kpss_long > kpss_cv)

ar_g    <- function(v, form, col) ar_ur_tbl[[col]][ar_ur_tbl$series == v & ar_ur_tbl$form == form]
ar_lv   <- ar_ur_tbl |> filter(form == "Level")
ar_dfs  <- ar_ur_tbl |> filter(form != "Level")
```

In levels, no ADF statistic reaches the 5% critical value of `r ar_f(ar_ur_tbl$adf_cv[1])`, and every short-bandwidth KPSS statistic exceeds its 5% critical value of `r ar_f(ar_ur_tbl$kpss_cv[1], 3)`, though none reaches the 1% value of `r ar_f(ar_ur_tbl$kpss_cv1[1], 3)`. In first differences, both tests indicate stationarity for all three series. The KPSS rejections are also sensitive to the bandwidth. With the long bandwidth, the level statistics fall to `r ar_f(ar_g("Inflation","Level","kpss_long"),3)`, `r ar_f(ar_g("Unemployment","Level","kpss_long"),3)` and `r ar_f(ar_g("Treasury","Level","kpss_long"),3)`, and `r c("none", "only some", "all")[1 + any(ar_lv$kpss_long_reject) + all(ar_lv$kpss_long_reject)]` reject. The long bandwidth trades power for size, so this doesn't show the series are stationary, but it does mean the KPSS evidence against stationarity is weak for every series.

**Structural change.** Applied to raw inflation, PELT finds the `r ar_n_raw` breaks reported in Stage 1, about one every `r round(160 / (ar_n_raw + 1))` quarters, which looks more like PELT tracking a wandering series than like a few regimes. The reason is that `cpt.mean()` assumes unit noise variance, while inflation's quarter-to-quarter noise has a standard deviation of about `r ar_f(ar_pi_scale)` points, so the BIC penalty is too small for the scale of the data. We therefore divide inflation by a robust estimate of its noise scale, $\text{MAD}(\Delta\pi_t)/\sqrt{2}$, before running PELT, which changes the Stage 1 settings. The rescaled analysis finds `r ar_n_scaled` breaks (@fig-ariel-levels). They describe inflation near `r ar_f(ar_segs$mean[1], 1)`% through 1965, about `r ar_f(ar_segs$mean[2], 1)`% through 1972, a high and volatile 1973–81 with segment means between `r ar_f(min(ar_high), 1)`% and `r ar_f(max(ar_high), 1)`%, and a lower level after 1981, with segment means of `r ar_join_and(paste0(ar_f(ar_low, 1), "%"))`. These shifts matter for the tests, since a series that is stationary around a mean that shifts a few times can make the ADF test fail to reject and the KPSS test reject (Perron 1989), which is exactly the pattern in levels above. Ignoring the shifts could lead us to treat inflation as having a unit root when it may instead be reverting to a slowly changing level. We don't use PELT for unemployment or the bill rate. Their quarter-to-quarter changes are small relative to their slow swings, so even after the same rescaling PELT splits them into `r min(ar_n_other) + 1` to `r max(ar_n_other) + 1` segments, which describes persistence rather than separate regimes.

\needspace{16\baselineskip}

```{r tbl-ariel-stationarity}
#| tbl-cap: "Stationarity summary, 1960Q1–1999Q4. ADF entries are $\\tau$ statistics with the BIC-selected lag, and KPSS entries are test statistics with the short bandwidth unless marked long. 5% critical values are -2.88 (ADF) and 0.463 (KPSS)."
#| tbl-colwidths: [17, 23, 26, 21, 13]
ar_dec <- function(x) ifelse(x, "reject", "do not reject")
ar_ev  <- function(v, form) paste0(ar_f(ar_g(v, form, "adf")), ", lag ", ar_g(v, form, "lag"),
                                " (", ar_dec(ar_g(v, form, "adf_reject")), ")")

tibble(
  Series = c("CPI inflation", "Unemployment", "Treasury bill rate"),
  `ADF evidence` = sapply(names(ar_series_labels), function(v)
    paste0("Level ", ar_ev(v, "Level"), ". Difference ",
           ar_ev(v, "First difference"), ".")),
  `KPSS evidence` = sapply(names(ar_series_labels), function(v)
    paste0("Level ", ar_f(ar_g(v, "Level", "kpss"), 3), " (",
           ar_dec(ar_g(v, "Level", "kpss_reject")), "), long ",
           ar_f(ar_g(v, "Level", "kpss_long"), 3), " (",
           ar_dec(ar_g(v, "Level", "kpss_long_reject")), "). Difference ",
           ar_f(ar_g(v, "First difference", "kpss"), 3), " (",
           ar_dec(ar_g(v, "First difference", "kpss_reject")), ").")),
  `Structural-change evidence` = c(
    paste(ar_n_scaled, "mean breaks after rescaling. Low early 1960s, high 1973–81, lower after 1981."),
    "No discrete regimes. Long cyclical swings.",
    "No discrete regimes. Rises with inflation, 1979–82 spike."),
  Classification = c("Unresolved", "$I(1)$", "$I(1)$")
) |>
  kable()
```

**Classification.** We classify unemployment and the Treasury bill rate as $I(1)$. The ADF test never rejects, differencing removes the persistence, and their lag-1 autocorrelations of `r ar_f(ar_acf_at("Unemployment", 1))` and `r ar_f(ar_acf_at("Treasury", 1))` decay only slowly, so a unit root is the simpler description even though the KPSS evidence is weak. Both rates are bounded in the long run, so we read $I(1)$ as a description of their behavior over this sample rather than a claim about their true process. We classify inflation as unresolved. Its unit-root tests look like those of the two rates, but its persistence is much lower, with a lag-1 autocorrelation of `r ar_f(ar_acf_at("Inflation", 1))` that falls to `r ar_f(ar_acf_at("Inflation", 8))` by lag 8, and its mean shifts at identifiable dates that group into three broad regimes, a low early 1960s, a high 1973–81 and a lower level after 1981. A series that is stationary around a shifting mean produces the same test results, while the two rates move too persistently for a few mean shifts to explain them. That is why the AR models in 4.4.3 and 4.4.4 are worth comparing against the gap models in 4.4.5, since the AR models impose one fixed long-run mean and the gap models track a local one. The forecasts will show which description of inflation works better out of sample.


\needspace{14\baselineskip}

## 4.3 Set up the expanding-window forecast experiment

```{r kc-design}
# Origins and targets by horizon [W4S2P15, W4S2P16]
kc_q     <- quarterly_data$Quarter
kc_first <- which(kc_q == tsibble::yearquarter("1999 Q4"))
kc_last  <- which(kc_q == tsibble::yearquarter("2019 Q4"))

kc_design <- tibble(h = kc_horizons) |>
  mutate(first_origin = kc_qlab(kc_q[kc_first]),
         last_origin  = kc_qlab(kc_q[kc_last - h]),
         targets      = paste0(kc_qlab(kc_q[kc_first + h]), "–", kc_qlab(kc_q[kc_last])),
         n            = kc_last - h - kc_first + 1)
stopifnot(identical(kc_design$n, c(80, 77, 73)))
kc_n_at <- function(hh) kc_design$n[kc_design$h == hh]
```

A forecast origin $T$ is the quarter a forecast is made in and the last quarter of its estimation sample. The first origin is 1999Q4, so every model is first fit on 1960Q1–1999Q4 and forecasts $h=1$, $h=4$, and $h=8$ quarters ahead. We then add one quarter, refit, and forecast again until the targets reach 2019Q4. Lag selection and the local mean are redone inside each origin's sample too, so nothing after $T$ is ever used.

| Forecast origin | Data used at that origin | $h=1$ target | $h=4$ target | $h=8$ target |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1999Q4 | 1960Q1–1999Q4 | 2000Q1 | 2000Q4 | 2001Q4 |
| 2000Q1 | 1960Q1–2000Q1 | 2000Q2 | 2001Q1 | 2002Q1 |

```{r tbl-kc-design}
#| tbl-cap: "Forecast origins, targets, and number of errors by horizon."
kc_design |>
  transmute(Horizon = paste0("$h=", h, "$"), `First origin` = first_origin,
            `Last origin` = last_origin, `Target period` = targets,
            `Number of errors` = n) |>
  kable(align = "lllll")
```

The forecast error is

$$
e_{j,t}^{(h)}=\pi_t-\widehat\pi_{j,t\mid t-h}^{(h)},
$$

so a positive error means the model underpredicted. This gives `r kc_n_at(1)`, `r kc_n_at(4)`, and `r kc_n_at(8)` errors per model at $h=1$, $h=4$, and $h=8$ (@tbl-kc-design), since longer horizons run out of targets sooner.

Sources: [W4S2P15, W4S2P16, W4S2P18]


\needspace{10\baselineskip}

## 4.4 Implement the core forecasting models

We compare seven models. The random walk and four-quarter average are benchmarks with nothing to estimate, and the other five forecast from estimated or constructed relationships. Each one is written as `fc_<model>(data, H)`, so the framework in 4.3 runs all seven the same way.

### 4.4.1 Random-walk model

The random walk without drift treats each quarter's inflation as last quarter's inflation plus an unpredictable shock:

$$
\pi_t=\pi_{t-1}+\varepsilon_t,
\qquad
E(\varepsilon_t)=0,
\qquad
Var(\varepsilon_t)=\sigma_\varepsilon^2.
$$

Since future shocks have mean zero, the best forecast at origin $T$ is the most recent observation at every horizon:

$$
\widehat\pi_{T+h\mid T}^{RW}=\pi_T,
\qquad h=1,\dots,8.
$$

In code, `fc_rw(data, H)` returns `data$Inflation[nrow(data)]` for every horizon $H$, using only the sample through $T$. The model has no parameters to estimate, so "re-estimating" it at each origin just means reading off the latest inflation rate, which makes it the simplest reference in the comparison. It never reverts toward any mean, which is where it parts company with a stationary AR, and it reacts fully to whatever happened in the last quarter, including noise.


### 4.4.2 Four-quarter-average benchmark

The four-quarter-average benchmark is used as a benchmark to be beaten by more complex models. In this naive method, the four most recently observed quarters are averaged to smooth out the noise in any one quarter, and this average is used as the forecast at every horizon. This estimate can be mathematically represented as

$$
\widehat\pi_{T+h\mid T}^{4Q}
=\frac14\sum_{j=0}^{3}\pi_{T-j},
$$

where $T$ is the most recently observed quarter and $h$ is the forecast horizon. In code, `fc_4q(data, H)` returns the mean of the last four inflation values in the origin's sample at every horizon. Its RMSE is the denominator for every relative RMSE in 4.5.

```{r david-4q-average}
# - bug fixed from david's: removed setwd(".."), which broke paths when rendering from the root.
fc_4q <- function(data, H) {
  mean(tail(data$Inflation, 4))
}
```


### 4.4.3 AR($p$) model

<!-- - bug fixed from kathy's: escaped the braces in p \in {1, 2, 3, 4} so they
render. -->

The AR($p$) model forecasts inflation using its own past values. Unlike the four-quarter average, which gives the same forecast at every horizon, the AR($p$) model uses current and lagged inflation to make forecasts that change with the horizon. At each forecast origin, we estimate autoregressive models with lag orders $p\in\{1, 2, 3, 4\}$ by maximum likelihood and select the model with the lowest Bayesian Information Criterion (BIC). The model is specified as

$$
\pi_t =c+\sum_{j=1}^{p}\phi_j\pi_{t-j}+\varepsilon_t,
$$

where $c$ is the intercept, $\phi_j$ are the autoregressive coefficients, and $\varepsilon_t$ is the error term. All four candidates are fit by exact maximum likelihood on the full sample through the origin, so their BIC values are comparable. Multistep forecasts are generated iteratively using the same estimated coefficients. If the model is stationary, forecasts converge toward its implied long-run mean. In code, `fc_arp(data, H)` fits the four candidates with `arima()`, keeps the one with the lowest BIC and returns its $H$-step forecast from `predict()`.

```{r kathy-ar-p}
# - bug fixed from kathy's: chunk didn't run
fc_arp <- function(data, H) {
  x <- data$Inflation
  # estimate AR(1) through AR(4)
  models <- lapply(1:4, function(p) {
    stats::arima(
      x,
      order = c(p, 0, 0),
      method = "ML")
  })
  # select the model with the lowest BIC
  bic_values <- sapply(models, BIC)
  best_model <- models[[which.min(bic_values)]]
  # forecast the next H quarters and keep the H-step value
  stats::predict(best_model, n.ahead = H)$pred[H]
}
```


### 4.4.4 Direct AR model

```{r kc-direct-diag}
# Lag length and unemployment coefficient for each direct forecast
kc_diag <- bind_rows(lapply(kc_horizons, function(hh) {
  bind_rows(lapply(kc_first:(kc_last - hh), function(i) {
    pi_T <- quarterly_data$Inflation[seq_len(i)]
    u_T  <- quarterly_data$Unemployment[seq_len(i)]
    ar   <- direct_fit(pi_T, hh)
    pc   <- direct_fit(pi_T, hh, u = u_T)
    tibble(origin = kc_q[i], h = hh,
           model  = c("Direct AR", "Direct Phillips curve"),
           refit  = c(ar$forecast, pc$forecast),
           p      = c(ar$p, pc$p),
           lambda = c(ar$lambda, pc$lambda))
  }))
}))

kc_p_text <- function(m, hh, first = FALSE) {
  ps <- kc_diag$p[kc_diag$model == m & kc_diag$h == hh]
  if (length(unique(ps)) == 1) paste0("$p_h=", ps[1], "$ at every origin")
  else paste0(if (first) "$p_h$ " else "", "between ", min(ps), " and ", max(ps))
}
```

The direct AR fits a separate regression for each horizon instead of iterating one equation forward.

$$
\pi_{t+h}=c_h+\sum_{j=0}^{p_h-1}\phi_{h,j}\,\pi_{t-j}+\varepsilon_{t+h}.
$$

At origin $T$, we only use rows with $t+h\le T$, so the response is already observed. We pick $p_h$ from 1 to 4 by BIC on a common set of rows, and the forecast plugs $\pi_T,\dots,\pi_{T-p_h+1}$ into the chosen equation. BIC picks `r kc_p_text("Direct AR", 1, first = TRUE)` for $h=1$, `r kc_p_text("Direct AR", 4)` for $h=4$, and `r kc_p_text("Direct AR", 8)` for $h=8$.

Sources: [W4S1P23, W4S1P24, W4S2P16, W4S2P18, W6S2P12, W7S2P33]

### 4.4.5 Local mean by exponential smoothing

Following Faust and Wright (2013), we estimate a slowly changing local mean $\tau_t$ by simple exponential smoothing with $\alpha=0.05$, a weight the project fixes rather than estimates. We start the recursion at the first observation and update one quarter at a time:

$$
\tau_{1960Q1}=\pi_{1960Q1},
\qquad
\tau_t=0.95\,\tau_{t-1}+0.05\,\pi_t,
\qquad
g_t=\pi_t-\tau_t .
$$

Each new quarter moves the local mean only 5% of the way toward current inflation, so $\tau_t$ follows sustained changes in the level but largely ignores one-quarter spikes. Unrolling the recursion shows that $\tau_t$ is a weighted average of current and past inflation with weights $0.05(0.95)^j$, which halve roughly every 13.5 quarters. The starting value $\tau_{1960Q1}=\pi_{1960Q1}$ is a single noisy observation, but its weight in $\tau_t$ is $0.95^{t-1}$, which is `r ar_f(0.95^40)` by 1970Q1 and `r formatC(0.95^159, format = "f", digits = 4)` by the first forecast origin, so the initialization has no practical effect on the local mean during the forecast period. The gap $g_t$ measures how far inflation sits above or below that local level.

```{r ariel-tau-checks}
# Guide example: previous tau 3.0, current inflation 5.0 -> tau 3.1, gap 1.9
ar_ex_tau <- 0.95 * 3.0 + 0.05 * 5.0
stopifnot(isTRUE(all.equal(ar_ex_tau, 3.1)), isTRUE(all.equal(5.0 - ar_ex_tau, 1.9)))

# One-sidedness: tau computed on data through 1999Q4 equals the full-sample
# tau over the same quarters, so tau_T never uses information after T.
ar_hist_sample <- ar_quarterly |> filter(date <= as.Date("2019-12-01"))
ar_full_tau    <- local_mean(ar_hist_sample$Inflation)
ar_origin_tau  <- local_mean(ar_initial$Inflation)
ar_one_sided   <- identical(ar_origin_tau, ar_full_tau[seq_along(ar_origin_tau)])
stopifnot(ar_one_sided)

ar_lm_hist <- add_local_mean(ar_hist_sample)
ar_tau_at  <- function(qtr) ar_lm_hist$tau[ar_lm_hist$Quarter == tsibble::yearquarter(qtr)]
ar_gap_at  <- function(qtr) ar_lm_hist$gap[ar_lm_hist$Quarter == tsibble::yearquarter(qtr)]
```

The recursion is one-sided because $\tau_t$ depends only on $\pi_t$ and earlier values. At each forecast origin $T$, `add_local_mean()` runs the update from 1960Q1 through $T$ on the origin's own sample, so $\tau_T$ and $g_T$ use nothing after $T$. As a check, the local mean computed from data through 1999Q4 matches the 1960Q1–1999Q4 portion of the local mean computed through 2019Q4 exactly. The function also reproduces the guide's example, where a previous local mean of 3.0 and current inflation of 5.0 give $\tau_t=3.1$ and $g_t=1.9$.

```{r fig-ariel-tau}
#| fig-cap: "Inflation and its exponentially smoothed local mean (top), and the inflation gap (bottom), 1960Q1–2019Q4. Values through any origin T are the ones available at T."
#| fig-height: 4.4
ar_lm_hist |>
  as_tibble() |>
  transmute(date,
            `Inflation and local mean` = Inflation,
            tau,
            `Inflation gap` = gap) |>
  pivot_longer(c(`Inflation and local mean`, `Inflation gap`),
               names_to = "panel") |>
  mutate(tau = ifelse(panel == "Inflation and local mean", tau, NA),
         panel = factor(panel, c("Inflation and local mean", "Inflation gap"))) |>
  ggplot(aes(date)) +
  geom_hline(data = tibble(panel = factor("Inflation gap",
                             c("Inflation and local mean", "Inflation gap")),
                           y = 0),
             aes(yintercept = y), linewidth = 0.3) +
  geom_line(aes(y = value), linewidth = 0.35, colour = "grey35") +
  geom_line(aes(y = tau), linewidth = 0.9, colour = "firebrick", na.rm = TRUE) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = as.Date("1999-12-01"), linetype = "dotted") +
  facet_wrap(~ panel, ncol = 1, scales = "free_y") +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Percent",
       title = "Local mean (alpha = 0.05) and inflation gap",
       subtitle = "Red line: local mean. Dotted line: first forecast origin, 1999Q4")
```

@fig-ariel-tau shows how the local mean behaves. It climbs from `r ar_f(ar_tau_at("1965 Q1"), 1)`% in 1965Q1 to a peak of `r ar_f(max(ar_lm_hist$tau), 1)`% in `r kc_qlab(ar_lm_hist$Quarter[which.max(ar_lm_hist$tau)])`, then declines slowly to `r ar_f(ar_tau_at("1999 Q4"), 1)`% at the first forecast origin and `r ar_f(ar_tau_at("2019 Q4"), 1)`% by 2019Q4. It lags turning points by several years, since the weight on new data is small. For example, the gap is `r ar_f(ar_gap_at("1980 Q1"), 1)` points in 1980Q1, when inflation surged well above the slowly rising local mean, and the local mean is still above inflation for much of the 1980s. Through the 1990s inflation is lower and steadier than the local mean, so the gap is mostly negative while the local mean drifts down to meet it. By the 2000s the gap is centered close to zero, with an average of `r ar_f(mean(ar_lm_hist$gap[year(ar_lm_hist$date) >= 2000]))` over 2000Q1–2019Q4. The gap is also less persistent than inflation itself. Its lag-1 autocorrelation over 1960Q1–1999Q4 is `r ar_f(acf(add_local_mean(ar_initial)$gap, lag.max = 1, plot = FALSE)$acf[2])`, compared with `r ar_f(ar_acf_at("Inflation", 1))` for inflation.

The gap AR (4.4.6) and the fixed-persistence forecast (4.4.7) call `add_local_mean()` on each origin's sample and read $\tau_T$ and $g_T$ from the last row. Both forecasts hold the local mean at $\tau_T$, since the future inflation needed to update it isn't observed yet.


### 4.4.6 Gap AR model

The gap AR model forecasts inflation in two parts: the slowly changing local mean $\tau_t$ from 4.4.5, and the inflation gap $g_t=\pi_t-\tau_t$ around it. At each forecast origin, we compute $\tau_t$ and $g_t$ from the origin's own sample and fit an autoregression with an intercept to the gap,

$$
g_t=a+\sum_{j=1}^{p}\rho_jg_{t-j}+v_t,
$$

by OLS for each $p\in\{1,2,3,4\}$, keeping the lag order with the lowest BIC. All four regressions use the same estimation sample, starting in the fifth quarter, so their BIC values are comparable. We then forecast the gap iteratively, feeding each forecast back in as a lag,

$$
\widehat g_{T+k\mid T}=\hat a+\sum_{j=1}^{p}\hat\rho_j\,\widehat g_{T+k-j\mid T},
\qquad k=1,\dots,h,
$$

where $\widehat g_{T+k-j\mid T}=g_{T+k-j}$ whenever $k-j\le 0$, and add the current local mean back:

$$
\widehat\pi_{T+h\mid T}^{GAP}
=\tau_T+\widehat g_{T+h\mid T}.
$$

The local mean is held at $\tau_T$ over the forecast period, since the future inflation needed to update it isn't observed yet. Comparing this model with the AR($p$) model shows whether recentering inflation around a slowly changing level improves forecasts. In code, `fc_gap_ar(data, H)` runs `add_local_mean()` from 4.4.5 on the origin's sample, fits the four gap autoregressions, and iterates the chosen one forward $H$ quarters.

```{r david-gap-ar}
fc_gap_ar <- function(data, H, max_p = 4) {
  d <- add_local_mean(data)
  g <- d$gap
  n <- length(g)

  idx  <- (max_p + 1):n                              # common sample for every p
  lags <- sapply(1:max_p, function(j) g[idx - j])    # column j is g_{t-j}
  fits <- lapply(1:max_p, function(p) lm(g[idx] ~ lags[, 1:p, drop = FALSE]))
  p    <- which.min(sapply(fits, BIC))
  b    <- coef(fits[[p]])                            # a, rho_1, ..., rho_p

  path <- tail(g, p)                                 # g_{T-p+1}, ..., g_T
  for (k in seq_len(H)) {
    path <- c(path, b[1] + sum(b[-1] * rev(tail(path, p))))
  }
  d$tau[n] + path[length(path)]
}
```


### 4.4.7 Fixed-persistence gap forecast

<!-- - bug fixed from kathy's: renumbered 4.4.6 -> 4.4.7, it clashed with
David's gap AR. -->

The fixed-persistence gap model forecasts inflation using the slowly changing local mean $\tau_t$ from 4.4.5 and the inflation gap $g_t = \pi_t-\tau_t$. Following Faust and Wright (2013), we fix the persistence coefficient at 0.46 rather than estimating it at each forecast origin. The forecast is specified as

$$
\widehat{\pi}_{T+h\mid T}^{FIX}
= \tau_T + 0.46^h g_T,
$$

where $T$ is the most recently observed quarter and $h$ is the forecast horizon. At each expanding-window origin, we calculate the local mean and gap using only the available observations. The local mean is held at $\tau_T$ over the forecast period, while the inflation gap shrinks geometrically toward zero as the horizon increases. Comparing this model with the estimated gap AR model shows whether estimating additional persistence parameters improves forecast accuracy enough to offset their estimation uncertainty. In code, `fc_fixed_gap(data, H)` runs `add_local_mean()` on the origin's sample and returns $\tau_T+0.46^H g_T$.

```{r kathy-fixed-gap}
fc_fixed_gap <- function(data, H, rho = 0.46) {
  data <- add_local_mean(data)
  tau_T <- tail(data$tau, 1)
  gap_T <- tail(data$gap, 1)

  forecast <- tau_T + rho^H * gap_T

  return(as.numeric(forecast))
}
```


### 4.4.8 Direct Phillips-curve model

```{r kc-lambda}
# Sign of the unemployment coefficient [W7S2P9, W9S2P30]
kc_lam <- kc_diag |>
  filter(model == "Direct Phillips curve") |>
  group_by(h) |>
  summarise(mean = mean(lambda), neg = mean(lambda < 0), .groups = "drop")
kc_lam_at  <- function(hh, col = "mean") kc_lam[[col]][kc_lam$h == hh]
kc_lam_pos <- kc_lam$h[kc_lam$mean > 0]
kc_lam_text <- if (length(kc_lam_pos) == 0) {
  "The negative sign fits the Phillips curve at every horizon."
} else if (kc_lam$mean[kc_lam$h == 1] < 0) {
  paste0("The negative sign at the shorter horizons fits the Phillips curve, but the sign flips at $h=",
         paste(kc_lam_pos, collapse = "$ and $h="),
         "$, so unemployment likely doesn't say much about inflation that far out.")
} else {
  "The coefficient doesn't have the negative sign the Phillips curve predicts."
}
```

The direct Phillips curve is the direct AR with the unemployment rate at $t$ added.

$$
\pi_{t+h}=c_h+\sum_{j=0}^{p_h-1}\phi_{h,j}\,\pi_{t-j}+\lambda_h u_t+\varepsilon_{t+h}.
$$

We keep $u_t$ in every equation, pick the inflation lags by BIC the same way, and forecast with $u_T$, which is already observed at the origin. The unemployment coefficient averages `r kc_f(kc_lam_at(1), 3)` at $h=1$, `r kc_f(kc_lam_at(4), 3)` at $h=4$, and `r kc_f(kc_lam_at(8), 3)` at $h=8$. `r kc_lam_text`

Sources: [W7S2P6, W7S2P9, W7S2P33, W9S2P30]

## 4.5 Evaluate the forecasts

```{r kc-run-all}
# Run all seven models through the expanding window (4.3)
kc_model_files <- c("Random walk"           = "rw",
                    "Four-quarter average"  = "4q",
                    "AR(p)"                 = "arp",
                    "Direct AR"             = "direct_ar",
                    "Gap AR"                = "gap_ar",
                    "Fixed-persistence gap" = "fixed_gap",
                    "Direct Phillips curve" = "direct_pc")

kc_all_fc <- run_expanding_window(
  quarterly_data,
  models = list("Random walk"           = fc_rw,
                "Four-quarter average"  = fc_4q,
                "AR(p)"                 = fc_arp,
                "Direct AR"             = fc_direct_ar,
                "Gap AR"                = fc_gap_ar,
                "Fixed-persistence gap" = fc_fixed_gap,
                "Direct Phillips curve" = fc_direct_pc),
  horizons = kc_horizons) |>
  attach_actuals(quarterly_data)

# Check 80 / 77 / 73 errors at h = 1 / 4 / 8
stopifnot(all(count(kc_all_fc, model, h)$n == rep(c(80L, 77L, 73L), 7)))

# Direct forecasts should match 4.4.4 and 4.4.8
kc_chk_direct <- kc_all_fc |>
  filter(model %in% c("Direct AR", "Direct Phillips curve")) |>
  inner_join(kc_diag, by = c("origin", "h", "model"))
stopifnot(nrow(kc_chk_direct) == 460,
          isTRUE(all.equal(kc_chk_direct$forecast, kc_chk_direct$refit)))

# Save each model to killian/outputs/
dir.create("killian/outputs", showWarnings = FALSE, recursive = TRUE)
for (m in names(kc_model_files)) {
  write_csv(filter(kc_all_fc, model == m),
            paste0("killian/outputs/forecasts_", kc_model_files[[m]], ".csv"))
}

# Compare with teammates' files in outputs/, print a note if they differ
for (m in names(kc_model_files)) {
  f <- paste0("outputs/forecasts_", kc_model_files[[m]], ".csv")
  if (!file.exists(f)) next
  theirs <- read_csv(f, show_col_types = FALSE, col_types = cols(origin = "c")) |>
    transmute(origin = tsibble::yearquarter(origin), h, theirs = forecast) |>
    inner_join(filter(kc_all_fc, model == m), by = c("origin", "h"))
  if (nrow(theirs) != sum(kc_all_fc$model == m) ||
      !isTRUE(all.equal(theirs$theirs, theirs$forecast))) {
    cat("NOTE: ", f, " does not match the forecasts in this report for ", m, ".\n",
        sep = "", file = stderr())
  }
}
```

We run all seven models through the same expanding window and compute the following for each model $j$ and horizon $h$.

$$
RMSE_{j,h}=\sqrt{\frac{1}{n_h}\sum_t\left(e_{j,t}^{(h)}\right)^2},
\qquad
rRMSE_{j,h}=\frac{RMSE_{j,h}}{RMSE_{4Q,h}},
$$

$$
MAE_{j,h}=\frac{1}{n_h}\sum_t\left|e_{j,t}^{(h)}\right|,
\qquad
ME_{j,h}=\frac{1}{n_h}\sum_te_{j,t}^{(h)}.
$$

RMSE is the main ranking measure, and a relative RMSE below 1 means the model beats the four-quarter average.

Sources: [W4S2P8, W4S2P9, W4S2P10, W4S2P18]

### 4.5.1 Random-walk forecasts

```{r ariel-rw-forecasts}
# - changed from ariel's: forecasts and 4Q benchmark come from the shared run
#   in 4.5. The rest is her code, with the 4Q join by origin and h.
ar_horizons <- c(1, 4, 8)

# Random-walk forecasts from the shared run above. The relative-RMSE column
# uses the 4.4.2 benchmark forecasts made at the same origins.
ar_rw_fc <- kc_all_fc |> filter(model == "Random walk")
ar_avg4  <- kc_all_fc |>
  filter(model == "Four-quarter average") |>
  select(origin, h, ar_avg4 = forecast)

ar_rw_acc <- ar_rw_fc |>
  left_join(ar_avg4, by = c("origin", "h")) |>
  group_by(h) |>
  summarise(n = n(),
            RMSE = sqrt(mean(error^2)),
            RMSE_4Q = sqrt(mean((actual - ar_avg4)^2)),
            MAE = mean(abs(error)),
            ME = mean(error),
            first = first(target), last = last(target), .groups = "drop") |>
  mutate(rRMSE = RMSE / RMSE_4Q,
         sqrt_h = RMSE[h == 1] * sqrt(h))   # RMSE implied by a random walk

# RMSE excluding 2008-2009 targets, as a robustness check on the sqrt(h) point
ar_rmse_ex0809 <- ar_rw_fc |>
  filter(!year(as.Date(target)) %in% c(2008, 2009)) |>
  group_by(h) |>
  summarise(RMSE = sqrt(mean(error^2)), .groups = "drop")

ar_rw_acc |>
  transmute(Horizon = h, `Target period` = paste0(kc_qlab(first), "–", kc_qlab(last)),
            `$n_h$` = n, RMSE = ar_f(RMSE), `Relative RMSE` = ar_f(rRMSE),
            MAE = ar_f(MAE), `Mean error` = ar_f(ME)) |>
  kable(align = "rlrrrrr",
        caption = "Random-walk forecast accuracy, targets through 2019Q4.")

ar_ra <- function(hh, col) ar_rw_acc[[col]][ar_rw_acc$h == hh]
ar_rx <- function(hh) ar_rmse_ex0809$RMSE[ar_rmse_ex0809$h == hh]

# Random-walk errors telescope: each is pi_{T+h} - pi_T, so their sum is the
# last h targets minus the first h origins.
ar_telescoped <- sapply(ar_horizons, function(hh) {
  d <- ar_rw_fc |> filter(h == hh)
  (sum(tail(d$actual, hh)) - sum(head(d$forecast, hh))) / nrow(d)
})
stopifnot(isTRUE(all.equal(ar_telescoped, ar_rw_acc$ME)))
ar_pi_q <- function(qtr) ar_quarterly$Inflation[ar_quarterly$Quarter == tsibble::yearquarter(qtr)]
ar_big <- ar_rw_fc |> filter(h == 1) |> slice_max(abs(error), n = 1)
ar_one_step <- ar_rw_fc |> filter(h == 1)
ar_share_0809 <- with(ar_one_step, sum(error[year(as.Date(target)) %in% c(2008, 2009)]^2) / sum(error^2))
```

We generate the random-walk forecasts at every origin from 1999Q4 to 2019Q3, keep $h=1,4,8$, and evaluate them against targets through 2019Q4, which gives `r ar_ra(1,"n")`, `r ar_ra(4,"n")` and `r ar_ra(8,"n")` forecast errors, matching the counts in the guide. The relative RMSE below uses the 4.4.2 benchmark forecasts from the same origins.

Relative RMSE against the four-quarter-average benchmark is `r ar_f(ar_ra(1,"rRMSE"))` at $h=1$, `r ar_f(ar_ra(4,"rRMSE"))` at $h=4$ and `r ar_f(ar_ra(8,"rRMSE"))` at $h=8$, so the random walk's RMSE runs `r sprintf("%.0f", 100 * (min(ar_rw_acc$rRMSE) - 1))` to `r sprintf("%.0f", 100 * (max(ar_rw_acc$rRMSE) - 1))` percent above the benchmark's, with the gap widest at $h=`r ar_rw_acc$h[which.max(ar_rw_acc$rRMSE)]`$. In levels, RMSE is `r ar_f(ar_ra(1,"RMSE"))` at $h=1$, `r ar_f(ar_ra(4,"RMSE"))` at $h=4$ and `r ar_f(ar_ra(8,"RMSE"))` at $h=8$, so accuracy barely changes with the horizon. The random walk carries the full noise of $\pi_T$ into every forecast, so even a one-quarter-ahead forecast inherits the volatility of the latest observation. The largest one-step error is `r ar_f(ar_big$error, 1)` points, for `r kc_qlab(ar_big$target)`, when the forecast carried forward `r kc_qlab(ar_big$origin)` inflation of `r ar_f(ar_big$forecast, 1)`% and actual inflation was `r ar_f(ar_big$actual, 1)`%. RMSE runs well above MAE at every horizon, `r ar_f(ar_ra(1,"RMSE"))` against `r ar_f(ar_ra(1,"MAE"))` at $h=1$, so a few very large errors drive much of the RMSE. Targets in 2008 and 2009 account for `r round(100 * ar_share_0809)`% of the squared one-step error, even though they're only 8 of the 80 quarters. Mean errors are close to zero (`r ar_f(ar_ra(1,"ME"))`, `r ar_f(ar_ra(4,"ME"))` and `r ar_f(ar_ra(8,"ME"))`), but for a random walk this is mechanical rather than evidence of no bias. Each error is the change in inflation from the origin to the target, so the errors telescope. At $h=1$ their mean is $(\pi_{2019Q4}-\pi_{1999Q4})/80=(`r ar_f(ar_pi_q("2019 Q4"))`-`r ar_f(ar_pi_q("1999 Q4"))`)/80\approx`r ar_f((ar_pi_q("2019 Q4") - ar_pi_q("1999 Q4")) / 80)`$, and at $h=4$ and $h=8$ the same cancellation leaves only the last $h$ targets and the first $h$ origins. A mean error near zero only says that inflation ended the evaluation sample close to where it started.

A random walk's $h$-step forecast error is the sum of $h$ independent shocks, so its RMSE should grow roughly as $\sqrt{h}$. From `r ar_f(ar_ra(1,"RMSE"))` at $h=1$, that implies about `r ar_f(ar_ra(4,"sqrt_h"))` at $h=4$ and `r ar_f(ar_ra(8,"sqrt_h"))` at $h=8$, far above the `r ar_f(ar_ra(4,"RMSE"))` and `r ar_f(ar_ra(8,"RMSE"))` we observe. The comparison isn't exact, since the targets overlap across origins and the 2008–09 errors reach every horizon, but dropping the 2008 and 2009 targets still leaves RMSE at `r ar_f(ar_rx(1))`, `r ar_f(ar_rx(4))` and `r ar_f(ar_rx(8))`, nowhere near $\sqrt{h}$ growth. The variance of the $h$-quarter change in inflation levels off rather than accumulating, so most quarter-to-quarter movement is transitory, which rules out a pure random walk. It doesn't settle the $I(0)$ versus $I(1)$ question from 4.2, though, since a slowly drifting $I(1)$ level plus large temporary noise produces the same flat profile. The local mean and gap in 4.4.5 separate exactly those two components, so the test of this reading is how the gap AR (4.4.6) and fixed-persistence forecasts (4.4.7) compare with the random walk and the AR models.


\needspace{14\baselineskip}

### 4.5.2 Direct AR and Phillips-curve forecasts

```{r kc-direct-accuracy}
# ME [W4S2P8], MAE and RMSE [W4S2P9], relative RMSE [W4S2P10]
kc_acc_all <- kc_all_fc |>
  group_by(model, h) |>
  summarise(n = n(),
            RMSE = sqrt(mean(error^2)),
            MAE  = mean(abs(error)),
            ME   = mean(error),
            first = first(target), last = last(target), .groups = "drop") |>
  group_by(h) |>
  mutate(rRMSE = RMSE / RMSE[model == "Four-quarter average"]) |>
  ungroup()

kc_acc <- kc_acc_all |> filter(model %in% c("Direct AR", "Direct Phillips curve"))

kc_acc |>
  transmute(Model = model, Horizon = h,
            `Target period` = paste0(kc_qlab(first), "–", kc_qlab(last)),
            `$n_h$` = n, RMSE = kc_f(RMSE), `Relative RMSE` = kc_f(rRMSE),
            MAE = kc_f(MAE), `Mean error` = kc_f(ME)) |>
  kable(align = "lrlrrrrr",
        caption = "Direct AR and direct Phillips-curve forecast accuracy, targets through 2019Q4.")

kc_ka <- function(m, hh, col) kc_acc[[col]][kc_acc$model == m & kc_acc$h == hh]
kc_pc_worse <- sum(kc_acc$RMSE[kc_acc$model == "Direct Phillips curve"] >
                     kc_acc$RMSE[kc_acc$model == "Direct AR"])
kc_big <- kc_all_fc |> filter(model == "Direct AR", h == 1) |> slice_max(abs(error), n = 1)

kc_beat_text <- if (all(kc_acc$rRMSE >= 1)) {
  "Neither direct model beats the four-quarter average at any horizon."
} else {
  paste0("The direct models beat the four-quarter average only for the ",
         kc_and(paste0(tolower(substr(kc_acc$model[kc_acc$rRMSE < 1], 1, 1)),
                       substring(kc_acc$model[kc_acc$rRMSE < 1], 2),
                       " at $h=", kc_acc$h[kc_acc$rRMSE < 1], "$")), ".")
}
kc_pc_text <- if (kc_pc_worse == 3) {
  "so adding unemployment doesn't help"
} else if (kc_pc_worse == 0) {
  "so adding unemployment helps at every horizon"
} else {
  paste0("so adding unemployment only helps at ", 3 - kc_pc_worse, " of the three horizons")
}
kc_me_dar <- kc_acc$ME[kc_acc$model == "Direct AR"]
kc_me_text <- if (all(kc_acc$ME < 0)) {
  "Both models also overpredict"
} else if (all(kc_acc$ME > 0)) {
  "Both models also underpredict"
} else {
  paste0(sum(kc_acc$ME < 0), " of the 6 mean errors are negative")
}
kc_me_trend <- if (all(diff(abs(kc_me_dar)) > 0)) "grows" else "goes"
```

`r kc_beat_text` The direct AR's relative RMSE is `r kc_and(kc_f(kc_acc$rRMSE[kc_acc$model == "Direct AR"]))` at $h=1$, $h=4$, and $h=8$, and the Phillips curve's is `r kc_and(kc_f(kc_acc$rRMSE[kc_acc$model == "Direct Phillips curve"]))`, `r kc_pc_text`. `r kc_me_text`, and the direct AR's mean error `r kc_me_trend` from `r kc_f(kc_ka("Direct AR", 1, "ME"))` at $h=1$ to `r kc_f(kc_ka("Direct AR", 8, "ME"))` at $h=8$. This likely comes from the long-run level each equation implies, which is estimated mostly from the higher inflation before 2000.

Sources: [W4S1P23, W4S2P8, W4S2P9, W4S2P10, W4S2P15, W4S2P18]


\needspace{24\baselineskip}

### 4.5.3 All seven models

```{r tbl-stage2-accuracy}
#| tbl-cap: "Expanding-window forecast accuracy for all seven models, targets through 2019Q4. Relative RMSE is against the four-quarter average. Models are sorted by RMSE within each horizon."
# - bug fixed from kathy's: renamed columns and filtered benchmark
kc_acc_all |>
  arrange(h, RMSE) |>
  transmute(Model = model, Horizon = h, `$n_h$` = n, RMSE = kc_f(RMSE),
            `Relative RMSE` = kc_f(rRMSE), MAE = kc_f(MAE), `Mean error` = kc_f(ME)) |>
  kable(align = "lrrrrrr")
```

```{r kc-horizon-text}
# Model names mid-sentence
kc_lab <- c("Random walk" = "random walk", "Four-quarter average" = "four-quarter average",
            "AR(p)" = "AR($p$)", "Direct AR" = "direct AR", "Gap AR" = "gap AR",
            "Fixed-persistence gap" = "fixed-persistence gap",
            "Direct Phillips curve" = "direct Phillips curve")

kc_best  <- kc_acc_all |> group_by(h) |> slice_min(RMSE, n = 1, with_ties = FALSE) |> ungroup()
kc_worst <- kc_acc_all |> group_by(h) |> slice_max(RMSE, n = 1, with_ties = FALSE) |> ungroup()

# Horizon summary from the table
kc_horizon_par <- function(hh) {
  d     <- kc_acc_all |> filter(h == hh) |> arrange(RMSE)
  bench <- d |> filter(model == "Four-quarter average")
  b1 <- d[1, ]; b2 <- d[2, ]; w <- d[nrow(d), ]
  mae1 <- d |> slice_min(MAE, n = 1, with_ties = FALSE)

  lead <- if (b1$model == "Four-quarter average") {
    paste0("no model beats the four-quarter average, which has the lowest RMSE (", kc_f(b1$RMSE), ").")
  } else {
    paste0("the ", kc_lab[b1$model], " has the lowest RMSE (", kc_f(b1$RMSE), "), ",
           kc_f(100 * (1 - b1$rRMSE), 1), "% below the four-quarter average (",
           kc_f(bench$RMSE), ")",
           if (b2$model == "Four-quarter average") ", which is second." else
             paste0(", and the ", kc_lab[b2$model], " is second (", kc_f(b2$RMSE), ")."))
  }
  mae <- if (kc_f(mae1$MAE) == kc_f(b1$MAE) && mae1$model != b1$model) {
    paste0("Its MAE (", kc_f(b1$MAE), ") ties the ", kc_lab[mae1$model],
           ", so its edge seems to come from avoiding a few big misses rather than from smaller typical errors.")
  } else if (mae1$model == b1$model) {
    paste0("It also has the lowest MAE (", kc_f(b1$MAE), "), so its typical errors are smaller too.")
  } else {
    paste0("The lowest MAE belongs to the ", kc_lab[mae1$model], " (", kc_f(mae1$MAE), ") rather than the leader (",
           kc_f(b1$MAE), "), so its edge seems to come from avoiding a few big misses rather than from smaller typical errors.")
  }
  me <- paste0("Its mean error of ", kc_f(b1$ME), " means it ",
               if (b1$ME < 0) "overpredicts" else "underpredicts", " on average.")
  worst <- paste0("The ", kc_lab[w$model], " is the worst, with a relative RMSE of ", kc_f(w$rRMSE), ".")
  paste0("At $h=", hh, "$, ", lead, " ", mae, " ", me, " ", worst)
}

kc_same_leader <- n_distinct(kc_best$model) == 1
kc_gain <- 100 * (1 - kc_best$rRMSE)
# The paragraph below assumes these hold. Rendering stops if they don't.
stopifnot(kc_same_leader, kc_best$model[1] == "Fixed-persistence gap",
          all(diff(kc_gain) > 0), n_distinct(kc_worst$model) == 1,
          all(kc_acc_all$RMSE[kc_acc_all$model == "Fixed-persistence gap"] <
              kc_acc_all$RMSE[kc_acc_all$model == "Gap AR"]))
kc_close_text <- if (kc_same_leader && kc_best$model[1] != "Four-quarter average") {
  paste0("The ", kc_lab[kc_best$model[1]],
         " has the lowest RMSE at all three horizons, and its edge over the benchmark ",
         if (all(diff(kc_gain) > 0)) "grows" else "changes", " with the horizon (",
         kc_and(paste0(kc_f(kc_gain, 1), "% at $h=", kc_best$h, "$")), ").",
         if (kc_best$model[1] == "Fixed-persistence gap")
           " Fixing the gap's persistence at 0.46 forecasts better than estimating it, which suggests the gap AR's extra parameters add more estimation noise than they gain in fit." else "")
} else {
  "The leading model changes with the horizon, so no single model dominates."
}
```

The `r kc_lab[kc_best$model[1]]` has the lowest RMSE at all three horizons (`r kc_and(kc_f(kc_best$RMSE))`), and its edge over the four-quarter average grows with the horizon (`r kc_and(paste0(kc_f(kc_gain, 1), "%"))`). The `r kc_lab[kc_worst$model[1]]` is the worst at every horizon, with relative RMSE from `r kc_f(min(kc_worst$rRMSE))` to `r kc_f(max(kc_worst$rRMSE))`. Since fixing the gap's persistence at 0.46 beats estimating it in the gap AR, the gap AR's extra parameters likely add more noise than they gain in fit.


\needspace{14\baselineskip}

## 4.6 Diagnose the leading one-step model

```{r kc-diag-refit}
# Best one-step estimated model (Models 3-7)
kc_core <- c("AR(p)", "Direct AR", "Gap AR", "Fixed-persistence gap", "Direct Phillips curve")
kc_lead <- kc_acc_all |> filter(h == 1, model %in% kc_core) |> slice_min(RMSE, n = 1)
# Refit below only works for the fixed-persistence gap
stopifnot(kc_lead$model == "Fixed-persistence gap")

# Refit through 2019Q4, residual is pi_t - (tau_{t-1} + 0.46 g_{t-1})
kc_res <- quarterly_data |>
  tsibble::filter_index(~ "2019 Q4") |>
  add_local_mean() |>
  as_tibble() |>
  mutate(fitted = lag(tau) + 0.46 * lag(gap),
         residual = Inflation - fitted) |>
  filter(!is.na(residual))

# Matches the 4.5 h = 1 errors over 2000Q1-2019Q4
kc_chk_res <- kc_all_fc |>
  filter(model == "Fixed-persistence gap", h == 1) |>
  inner_join(select(kc_res, target = Quarter, residual), by = "target")
stopifnot(nrow(kc_chk_res) == 80, isTRUE(all.equal(kc_chk_res$error, kc_chk_res$residual)))

kc_n_res <- nrow(kc_res)
```

Among the estimated models, the `r kc_lab[kc_lead$model]` has the lowest $h=1$ RMSE (`r kc_f(kc_lead$RMSE)`), so it's the one we diagnose. Refitting it through 2019Q4 gives `r kc_n_res` one-step residuals, $\pi_t-(\tau_{t-1}+0.46\,g_{t-1})$, from 1960Q2 to 2019Q4.

```{r fig-kc-resid}
#| fig-cap: "Fixed-persistence gap one-step residuals, 1960Q2–2019Q4."
#| fig-height: 2.6
ggplot(kc_res, aes(date, residual)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linewidth = 0.3) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.35) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Residual (points)",
       title = "Fixed-persistence gap residuals")
```

```{r fig-kc-resid-acf}
#| fig-cap: "Sample ACF of the residuals, lags 1–20. Dashed lines are approximate 95% bounds."
#| fig-height: 2.4
kc_acf   <- acf(kc_res$residual, lag.max = 20, plot = FALSE)
kc_acf_d <- tibble(lag = kc_acf$lag[-1], acf = kc_acf$acf[-1])
kc_bound <- 1.96 / sqrt(kc_n_res)
kc_sig   <- kc_acf_d$lag[abs(kc_acf_d$acf) > kc_bound]

ggplot(kc_acf_d, aes(lag, acf)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linewidth = 0.3) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = c(-1, 1) * kc_bound, linetype = "dashed", colour = "steelblue") +
  geom_segment(aes(xend = lag, yend = 0)) +
  labs(x = "Lag (quarters)", y = "ACF", title = "Autocorrelation of the residuals")
```

```{r kc-ljung-box}
# - bug fixed from kathy's: lag 12 -> 10, the course rule for nonseasonal
#   data [W6S2P21].
# l = min(10, T/5), df = l since nothing is estimated [W6S2P21]
kc_lb_lag <- min(10, floor(kc_n_res / 5))
kc_lb     <- Box.test(kc_res$residual, lag = kc_lb_lag, type = "Ljung-Box", fitdf = 0)
kc_lb_rej <- kc_lb$p.value < 0.05
kc_p_fmt  <- if (kc_lb$p.value < 0.001) "below 0.001" else paste("of", kc_f(kc_lb$p.value, 3))
```

<!-- - changed from kathy's: dropped the claim that inflation is nonstationary since 4.2 leaves it unresolved. -->

The residuals are centered near zero, but their spread clearly isn't constant, with the biggest swings in the 1970s, early 1980s, and 2000s and the largest residual in `r kc_qlab(kc_res$Quarter[which.max(abs(kc_res$residual))])`. `r if (length(kc_sig) == 0) "The ACF stays inside the 95% bounds through lag 20." else paste0("The ACF falls outside the 95% bounds at lag", if (length(kc_sig) > 1) "s " else " ", kc_and(kc_sig), ".")` Following the course rule $\ell=\min(10,T/5)=`r kc_lb_lag`$, the Ljung–Box statistic is `r kc_f(kc_lb$statistic)` with a p-value `r kc_p_fmt`, so we `r if (kc_lb_rej) "reject" else "don't reject"` the null of no autocorrelation. `r if (kc_lb_rej) "This means the fixed persistence of 0.46 doesn't capture all of the dependence in inflation." else "This means the fixed persistence of 0.46 leaves no detectable dependence."`

```{r fig-kc-rolling-sd}
#| fig-cap: "20-quarter rolling standard deviation of the residuals. Each point covers the 20 quarters ending in that quarter."
#| fig-height: 2.4
kc_roll <- tibble(date    = kc_res$date[20:kc_n_res],
                  Quarter = kc_res$Quarter[20:kc_n_res],
                  sd      = sapply(20:kc_n_res, function(i) sd(kc_res$residual[(i - 19):i])))

ggplot(kc_roll, aes(date, sd)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.4) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Rolling SD (points)",
       title = "Residual variability over time")

kc_roll_max <- kc_roll |> slice_max(sd, n = 1)
kc_roll_min <- kc_roll |> slice_min(sd, n = 1)
kc_sd_pre   <- sd(kc_res$residual[year(kc_res$date) < 2000])
kc_sd_post  <- sd(kc_res$residual[year(kc_res$date) >= 2000])
```

```{r tbl-kc-top5}
#| tbl-cap: "The five largest one-step residuals, 1960Q2–2019Q4."
kc_top5 <- kc_res |>
  mutate(sq = residual^2) |>
  slice_max(sq, n = 5)
kc_top5_share <- sum(kc_top5$sq) / sum(kc_res$residual^2)

kc_top5 |>
  transmute(Quarter = kc_qlab(Quarter), Inflation = kc_f(Inflation),
            Fitted = kc_f(fitted), Residual = kc_f(residual), `Squared residual` = kc_f(sq, 1)) |>
  kable(align = "lrrrr")
```

The 20-quarter rolling standard deviation ranges from `r kc_f(kc_roll_min$sd)` to `r kc_f(kc_roll_max$sd)`, so the error variance changes over time and intervals built from a single variance wouldn't be reliable. The five largest residuals (@tbl-kc-top5) also make up `r kc_f(100 * kc_top5_share, 1)`% of the sum of squared residuals, so a few quarters like `r kc_qlab(kc_top5$Quarter[1])` could decide the DM–HLN comparisons in the final project.

Sources: [W6S2P21, W6S2P23]


\needspace{14\baselineskip}

## 4.7 Summarize the Stage 2 results

```{r kc-summary}
# Summary of @tbl-stage2-accuracy by horizon
# ME [W4S2P8], MAE and RMSE [W4S2P9], relative RMSE [W4S2P10]
kc_best_text <- if (n_distinct(kc_best$model) == 1) {
  paste0("The ", kc_lab[kc_best$model[1]], " has the lowest RMSE at every horizon (",
         kc_and(paste0(kc_f(kc_best$RMSE), " at $h=", kc_best$h, "$")),
         "), so the leader doesn't change with the horizon")
} else {
  paste0("The lowest RMSE goes to the ",
         kc_and(paste0(kc_lab[kc_best$model], " at $h=", kc_best$h, "$ (", kc_f(kc_best$RMSE), ")")),
         ", so the leader changes with the horizon")
}

kc_beat_all <- kc_acc_all |> filter(model != "Four-quarter average", rRMSE < 1)
kc_beat_by_h <- sapply(kc_horizons, function(hh) {
  m <- kc_beat_all$model[kc_beat_all$h == hh]
  paste0(if (length(m)) paste0("the ", kc_and(kc_lab[m])) else "no model", " at $h=", hh, "$")
})
kc_beat_all_text <- paste0(paste(head(kc_beat_by_h, -1), collapse = ", "), ", and ",
                           tail(kc_beat_by_h, 1))
kc_worst_text <- if (n_distinct(kc_worst$model) == 1) {
  paste0("The ", kc_lab[kc_worst$model[1]], " is the worst at every horizon, with relative RMSE from ",
         kc_f(min(kc_worst$rRMSE)), " to ", kc_f(max(kc_worst$rRMSE)), ".")
} else {
  paste0("The worst model is the ",
         kc_and(paste0(kc_lab[kc_worst$model], " at $h=", kc_worst$h, "$")), ".")
}

# Lowest-MAE vs lowest-RMSE model
kc_mae_best <- kc_acc_all |> group_by(h) |> slice_min(MAE, n = 1, with_ties = FALSE) |> ungroup()
kc_mae_diff <- kc_mae_best |> filter(model != kc_best$model[match(h, kc_best$h)])
kc_mae_text <- if (nrow(kc_mae_diff) == 0) {
  "MAE picks the same leader as RMSE at every horizon"
} else {
  kc_mae_tie <- kc_f(kc_mae_diff$MAE) ==
    kc_f(kc_acc_all$MAE[match(paste(kc_best$model[match(kc_mae_diff$h, kc_best$h)], kc_mae_diff$h),
                              paste(kc_acc_all$model, kc_acc_all$h))])
  paste0("MAE picks the same leader as RMSE except at ",
         kc_and(paste0("$h=", kc_mae_diff$h, "$, where the ", kc_lab[kc_mae_diff$model],
                       ifelse(kc_mae_tie, " ties it (", " has the lowest MAE ("),
                       kc_f(kc_mae_diff$MAE), ")")))
}
kc_ratio   <- range(kc_acc_all$MAE / kc_acc_all$RMSE)
kc_big_all <- kc_all_fc |> filter(h == 1) |> group_by(target) |>
  summarise(miss = mean(abs(error)), .groups = "drop") |> slice_max(miss, n = 1)

kc_me_w  <- kc_acc_all |> filter(h == 8) |> slice_min(ME, n = 1)
kc_me_at <- function(m, hh) kc_f(kc_acc_all$ME[kc_acc_all$model == m & kc_acc_all$h == hh])
# Fixed-mean models pull long-horizon forecasts toward their mean [W4S1P23, W4S1P24]
kc_me_reason <- if (kc_me_w$model %in% c("AR(p)", "Direct AR", "Direct Phillips curve")) {
  "likely because its long-run level is estimated mostly from the higher inflation before 2000"
} else {
  "likely because its forecasts sit above the lower inflation of 2000 to 2019"
}

# One-paragraph summary. The wording assumes one leader that beats the
# four-quarter average at every horizon, one worst model, and mostly negative ME.
kc_lead_m <- kc_best$model[1]
stopifnot(n_distinct(kc_best$model) == 1, sum(kc_beat_all$model == kc_lead_m) == 3,
          n_distinct(kc_worst$model) == 1, sum(kc_acc_all$ME < 0) > nrow(kc_acc_all) / 2)
kc_others <- kc_beat_all |> filter(model != kc_lead_m)
kc_others_text <- if (nrow(kc_others) == 0) "" else {
  per <- sapply(split(kc_others$h, kc_others$model), function(hs) kc_and(paste0("$h=", hs, "$")))
  if (length(per) == 1) paste0(", while the ", kc_lab[names(per)], " also beats it at ", per)
  else paste0(", while the ", kc_and(paste0(kc_lab[names(per)], " (at ", per, ")")), " also beat it")
}
kc_sum_text <- paste0(
  "The ", kc_lab[kc_lead_m], " has the lowest RMSE at every horizon and beats the four-quarter average at all three",
  kc_others_text, ". The ", kc_lab[kc_worst$model[1]], " is the worst at every horizon. ",
  "MAE is only ", kc_f(100 * kc_ratio[1], 0), " to ", kc_f(100 * kc_ratio[2], 0),
  "% of RMSE, so a few big misses like ", kc_qlab(kc_big_all$target), " push RMSE up for every model. ",
  "Lastly, ", sum(kc_acc_all$ME < 0), " of the ", nrow(kc_acc_all),
  " model and horizon combinations have negative mean error, so overprediction is the norm from 2000 to 2019. ",
  "The DM–HLN tests come in the final project.")
```

`r kc_sum_text`

Sources: [W4S1P23, W4S1P24, W4S2P8, W4S2P9, W4S2P10, W4S2P18, W4S2P19]
